story.title: Iran's President Responds to Trump's Threat at UN General Assembly
story.summary: In a speech at the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian declared that Iran would not surrender following U.S. President Donald Trump's threat to 'annihilate' the Islamic Republic. Pezeshkian characterized Iran as a victim of U.S. terrorism, showcasing images of Iranian civilians affected by military actions. His address came amid ongoing conflict between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

timeline_highlights.title: Trump Issues Threats Against Iranian Infrastructure Amid Strait of Hormuz Tensions
timeline_highlights.summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened to target Iranian bridges and power plants in retaliation for any attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. He stated that for each ship fired upon by Iranian forces, the US would respond by destroying a corresponding piece of Iranian infrastructure. This escalation comes amid ongoing tensions in the region and rising oil prices.
key_facts: Trump threatened to destroy Iranian infrastructure for each ship attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The threat follows continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the region.
Oil prices have surged amid the escalating tensions.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The “Iran War” refers to the 2026 armed conflict between the United States and Iran, involving Israeli strikes and wider regional attacks, alongside recurring diplomatic efforts to halt hostilities. It has centered in part on security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, making the conflict consequential for Gulf states and global energy markets.

facts.label: Start of major hostilities
facts.value: The UN Secretary-General said that the United States and Israel launched major strikes against Iran on February 28, 2026, followed by Iranian attacks affecting Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. In a March 10 letter to the Security Council, the United States said it had begun combat operations on February 28 and characterized them as self-defense.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The core interstate conflict is between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, with Israel participating in the initial strikes and Gulf states affected by subsequent regional attacks. The Strait of Hormuz—between Iran and Oman and linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea—has been a central operational and diplomatic focus.

facts.label: Maritime and economic significance
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a major energy chokepoint: the U.S. Energy Information Administration has described it as the world’s most important oil-transit chokepoint because of the volumes of petroleum moving through it. UN reporting during the conflict said ship transits had fallen by more than 90% after the crisis escalated in late February 2026.

facts.label: Diplomatic track
facts.value: Ceasefire and negotiation efforts have accompanied the fighting. The UN welcomed a June 2026 U.S.-Iran peace arrangement calling for a permanent ceasefire, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further talks, while later UN briefings described the situation as fragile and noted renewed military exchanges in late June.

facts.label: Legal and U.S. constitutional framework
facts.value: Internationally, the UN Charter requires states to settle disputes peacefully and prohibits threats or uses of force inconsistent with the Charter; the law of the sea recognizes transit passage through straits used for international navigation. explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground and at sea?
explore_lenses.title: Hormuz has become a central pressure point
explore_lenses.summary: The UN speeches took place as the war’s effects extended beyond Iran’s territory to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Pezeshkian paired his defiance with a warning that unequal access to the waterway and an expanded military presence would not produce peace.

claims.text: Pezeshkian told the General Assembly that the Strait of Hormuz had become a focal point of U.S.-Iran tensions and said Iran could not accept others benefiting from the route while it was denied shipping access.

Before the UN meetings, a senior Iranian official said Iran could reopen Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and ended its blockade of Iranian ports; this was a reported proposal, not an agreed arrangement.

The UN human-rights office said the wider hostilities had affected 12 other states and damaged homes, airports and energy infrastructure; it also reported civilian casualties in Iran and Iranian missile and drone attacks on states across the region.

explore_lenses.title: Opposing accounts of war, nuclear risk and civilian harm
explore_lenses.summary: Washington says its campaign is meant to stop Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon and to counter Iranian-backed violence. Tehran characterizes the February 28 U.S.-Israeli attack and subsequent strikes as unlawful aggression, foregrounding civilian casualties and alleged attacks on protected sites.

claims.text: The White House said Trump’s UN address framed Iran as a terrorism sponsor and said U.S. policy would not allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s UN representative has stated that the war began on February 28, 2026, with U.S.-Israeli attacks; this is Iran’s official characterization of the conflict and responsibility for it.

The UN human-rights office called for a prompt, impartial and thorough investigation of the strike on a Minab primary school, noting reports that girls were killed and injured. It did not in that statement assign legal responsibility for the attack.

Iran has submitted UN documents alleging that U.S. missile strikes destroyed the Minab school and killed more than 168 students, but those documents present Iran’s account and casualty figures rather than an independently adjudicated finding.

explore_lenses.label: What diplomatic steps are actually confirmed?
explore_lenses.title: Indirect contacts resumed, but no deal is public
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate diplomatic development was not a U.S.-Iran presidential meeting but mediated, indirect communication on the UN sidelines. Both sides signaled interest in diplomacy while retaining incompatible public positions and military threats.

claims.text: Reuters reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators at the UN—the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire collapsed in July.
Trump described the engagement as a productive meeting with Iranian mediators, while Reuters reported that neither side publicly described a change in its negotiating position.
Pezeshkian said Iran would not surrender but believed diplomacy could help end the conflict, while Trump’s UN address presented a deal as an alternative to further escalation.

The UN General Assembly’s general debate was scheduled to continue through September 26 and resume September 28, providing a continuing venue for bilateral and mediated contacts but not a confirmed peace-negotiation timetable.

story_report.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used his address to the UN General Assembly to reject President Donald Trump’s threat to “annihilate” Iran. Pezeshkian said Iran would not surrender, described the country as a victim of U.S. terrorism and argued that diplomacy could help end the conflict. The competing public positions were aired as Iranian and U.S. representatives communicated through mediators at the UN, their first reported contacts since an interim ceasefire collapsed in July, although neither side publicly announced a change in its negotiating stance.

sections.heading: Hormuz Dispute and Regional Damage
sections.body: Pezeshkian said the Strait of Hormuz had become a focal point of tensions, arguing that Iran could not accept other countries benefiting from the route while it was denied shipping access. Before the UN meetings, a senior Iranian official proposed reopening the strait to Gulf shipping within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and ended its blockade of Iranian ports; the proposal was not an agreement. The UN human-rights office said the wider hostilities had affected 12 other states and damaged homes, airports and energy infrastructure, while causing civilian casualties in Iran and prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks across the region.

sections.heading: Washington and Tehran State Rival Accounts
sections.body: The White House said Trump’s UN address portrayed Iran as a sponsor of terrorism and maintained that U.S. policy would prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran’s UN representative has said the war began with U.S.-Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, 2026, an official Iranian characterization of responsibility for the conflict. Iran has also alleged in UN submissions that U.S. missile strikes destroyed a primary school in Minab and killed more than 168 students, while the UN human-rights office has called for a prompt, impartial investigation without assigning legal responsibility.

sections.heading: Mediated UN Contacts Continue
sections.body: Trump described the mediated engagement as productive, while Reuters reported that neither Washington nor Tehran publicly identified a shift in negotiating positions. Pezeshkian said Iran believed diplomacy could help end the conflict, and Trump presented a deal as an alternative to further escalation. The General Assembly’s debate was scheduled to continue through Sept. 26 and resume on Sept. 28, leaving a venue for further contacts but no confirmed peace-negotiation timetable.

unresolved.text: The operational status of the Strait of Hormuz, the specific terms of any U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and whether Washington would accept Iran’s proposed conditions for reopening the route had not been publicly settled as of Sept. 23.
No independent public findings had established responsibility, target selection or the full casualty record for the Minab school attack.
No public text had been released for a ceasefire, shipping agreement, sanctions arrangement or follow-up negotiating schedule.

related_stories.title: Tigray Forces Capture Airports Amid Renewed Fighting in Ethiopia
related_stories.summary: Tigrayan rebels have taken control of airports in northern Ethiopia and engaged in clashes with federal troops in the Afar region. This escalation marks a significant resurgence of conflict, with reports indicating that Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to three airports in Tigray, signaling a breakdown of the Pretoria Agreement that had previously ended the 2020-2022 war.

related_stories.title: Iran's President Declares Defiance at UN Amid Ongoing Tensions
related_stories.summary: In a defiant address at the UN General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian stated that Iran would 'never bend at the knee' and accused the US of terrorism. He emphasized that warfare transcends borders and asserted that the Strait of Hormuz would not be used to impose insecurity on Iran. Despite his calls for diplomacy, Iranian officials characterized discussions with US counterparts as unremarkable.

related_stories.title: US and Iran Engage in Productive Talks Amid Hopes for Progress
related_stories.summary: Recent shuttle talks between the US and Iran, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, have been described as 'productive.' The discussions involved Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who communicated through mediators. While the talks raised hopes for progress towards ending the ongoing conflict, no concessions were made during the discussions.

related_stories.title: Trump Administration Plans to Admit 17,500 South African Refugees in 2027
related_stories.summary: The Trump administration announced plans to admit up to 17,500 Afrikaners from South Africa to the United States in 2027. This decision is part of a new refugee policy aimed at addressing specific needs within the refugee population.
